transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-01
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Astra CTO), Liam O'Connor (ML Eng), Sara Gomez (Infra)
Agenda: quick intro, current stack + constraints, p95 targets, concurrency and streaming needs, token/sec benchmarking approach, next steps

Summary (auto-generated, optional):
Astra Logistics is evaluating Redwood for production inference. Primary concerns: meeting p95 latency targets for short conversational prompts (p95 < 200ms for 512-token-ish requests), burst concurrency up to 300 concurrent streams, token/sec throughput for batch reranking pipelines, and security (VPC/KMS/SOC2). They requested a dedicated-run benchmark and benchmark template.

00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining! quick intros, i'm maya from redwood, daniel's our se, and then over to you priya to intro the team
00:18 Priya (Astra CTO): hi yeah priya here, we run inference for route optimization and real-time dispatch, liam does the models and sara infra. our key ask is latency and predictability, our sla needs p95 under 250ms for the small chat calls and p95 under 1s for longer context ops
00:36 Liam (Astra ML Eng): and to add we do streaming responses to driver apps, so token/sec and partial responses matter a lot, we also do nightly batch reranks for route candidates so throughput matters there.
00:50 Daniel (Redwood SE): great, that aligns with what we've seen with logistics customers. can you share typical sequence lengths, concurrency patterns, and QPS? even rough numbers help.
01:05 Priya: sure, median seq len around 120 tokens, 95th around 480 for a fraction of calls, typical steady qps around 400 across regions, peak bursts to ~2k qps for promo periods, concurrent streaming sessions up to ~300 in worst cases
01:28 Maya: perfect — when you say streaming sessions, is that server-sent events / chunked SSE or websockets? and do you need partial decoding on device or server-side aggregation?
01:40 Sara (Infra): we use websockets right now, want partial decoded tokens streamed to the mobile app. we want low tail latency, jitter hurts UX. also note we run some workloads in our VPC, on-prem for sensitive customers.
02:00 Daniel: ok good context. a couple of quick clarifying q's: do you currently use any model provider? how much is in-house vs hosted?
02:10 Liam: currently we self-host a mix of open weights for privacy, but we've been hit by infra ops cost and some reliability during peaks. we also evaluate vertex and openai for overflow.
02:25 Maya: usual tradeoff. for p95 targets we ask about batching and prefix caching — do you have repeated prefixes like prompts that allow KV cache reuse?
02:36 Priya: yes, a lot of starters are templated, driver id and location, so prefix reuse is moderate. we've tried basic caching but it's ad-hoc.
02:46 Daniel: cool. for numbers, when you say p95 < 250ms, are you measuring from request arrival to first token or to final token?
02:53 Priya: good point — we want p95 to first token under 200ms for small prompts (<=128 tokens), and p95 to final token under 1s for 512 tokens.
03:05 Maya: makes sense. next i'll give a high-level of hosted vs dedicated vs private — and where latency wins/loses.
03:12 Maya: hosted = fastest to integrate, we have pre-warmed pools and auto-burst but multi-tenant so tail variability can happen. dedicated = you get reserved GPU pools and more predictable p95s with autoscale policies; private = full control in your VPC or on-prem but you manage infra and scaling.
03:40 Daniel: architecture-wise we do continuous batching, kv cache and optimized kernels. for streaming we avoid large batch windows to reduce first-token latency; we batch for throughput paths like rerank. quantization plays a role too, though some models degrade quality.
03:58 Liam: can you give example p95 numbers you've seen for similar seq lengths on dedicated?
04:05 Daniel: rough ballpark — for a 128-token request on rtx-8000-class or A100-like equivalent with optimized kernels and small batching, p95 to first token can be ~60–120ms in dedicated; end-to-end for 128 tokens p95 ~250–350ms depending on model and quantization. for 512 tokens p95 to final token can be closer to 800ms–1.2s. these are non-binding and depend on sequence distribution and batching.
04:40 Priya: that's helpful. our target to first token 200ms seems feasible then on dedicated, but we worry about concurrency and token/sec budgets.
04:50 Maya: good note — one lever is model selection and quantization: int8 or int4 gives large throughput wins but likely small quality delta. another is smart routing: route low-latency traffic to warmed hosts, fallback to cheaper nodes for non-critical batch jobs.
05:08 Liam: do you support prefix/KV cache across sessions? we need cache hits across a fleet, not just within one host.
05:16 Daniel: yes, we have global cache coordination for common prefixes, but hit rates depend on shard keys and session affinity. there's some nuance with private deployments and cross-host KV propagation.
05:30 Sara: on security, we need SOC2 plus KMS integration and optional HSM for keys, plus VPC peering. implications for routing and cross-region fallbacks?
05:42 Maya: we support KMS integration and have SOC2 and ISO docs we'll share. for VPC deployments you can opt for private control plane and we support VPC peering; routing fallbacks are policy-driven but you can limit cross-region movement for data residency.
05:58 Priya: excellent — please share those docs.
06:02 Maya: will do. next, can we talk about benchmarking? we usually send a benchmark template (csv + scripts) and run a dedicated benchmark with your prompts and sequence distribution. we can do hosted quick tests, but for strict p95 targets we recommend a dedicated reserved run to full-load test.
06:20 Priya: what's the difference in fidelity between a hosted smoke test and a dedicated run?
06:25 Daniel: hosted smoke tests are useful for functional validation; they approximate latency but are noisy due to multi-tenancy. dedicated runs on reserved capacity with pinned model versions and tuned kernel selection give much more representative tail latency and throughput numbers.
06:40 Liam: ok can you run token/sec estimates? we're seeing rerank jobs that need ~30k tokens/sec sustained to finish nightly windows.
06:48 Daniel: sure. rough estimate depends on model size and GPU type: with quantized 7B on an A100-like GPU you might get 10–15k tokens/sec per GPU for decode-heavy workloads; bigger models drop token/sec. for batching-heavy rerank you can often push higher by increasing batch sizes and using non-streaming decode (e.g., greedy). we'll put concrete numbers in the template.
07:15 Maya: for concurrency: with 300 concurrent streaming sessions, you need enough warm workers and small-batch scheduling to keep tails down; autoscaling cold starts can blow p95, so reserved pools or pre-warm policies help.
07:35 Priya: how do you charge for reserved capacity? we need monthly committed options and burst credits.
07:40 Maya: we have reserved capacity plans with monthly/annual commits; burst credits for overflow and an SLA for latency and uptime on dedicated tiers. i'll include pricing tiers and an example TCO model in the follow-up.
07:55 Liam: any gotchas with quantization and accuracy for our models? we have regression tolerance of 2% on top-k accuracy metrics.
08:05 Daniel: quantization can change outputs — we recommend running evals against your prompt sets. Redwood Optimize can suggest profiles and we'll surface quality regression alerts tied to evals.
08:22 Priya: good. can you walk through a sample benchmark run we should expect?
08:27 Daniel: sure - step 1: you provide sample prompts, seq length histogram, and traffic pattern (QPS + concurrency). step 2: we run an A/B benchmark across hosted/dedicated/pinned model variants with streaming and non-streaming modes. step 3: we measure p50/p95/p99 for first token and end-to-end, token/sec throughput, GPU utilization, and cost-per-1M tokens. step 4: we deliver a spreadsheet and recommendations.
09:05 Maya: we'll share the benchmark template (link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/astla-template.csv) and a short runbook.
09:12 Priya: excellent. we want to run a dedicated benchmark next week if possible; need to confirm cost.
09:18 Maya: i'll put options in the follow-up, and daniel will run a preliminary token/sec estimate to help size the reserved pool.
09:25 Liam: one more question on streaming: do you support partial response callbacks and per-token eventing to our websocket endpoints?
09:33 Daniel: yes, we support streaming over websockets and chunked http; you can configure chunk sizes, and we supply SDK hooks. note that very small chunk sizes increase overhead so there's a tradeoff.
09:47 Sara: operationally we are worried about KV cache warmup when scaling up — new replicas might have cold caches and spike latency. how do you mitigate?
09:56 Daniel: strategies: 1) pre-warm with synthetic traffic to seed KV caches; 2) stateful affinitized routing to prefer warmed hosts; 3) rapid state sync for hot prefixes. for private deployments you can also run a cache-sync service we provide.
10:20 Priya: great. let's recap next steps.
10:24 Maya: recap: 1) Maya send pricing/reserved options + SOC2/ISO + bench template; 2) Daniel run token/sec estimates and propose GPU counts for 300 concurrent streams and nightly 30k token/sec rerank; 3) Astra share seq hist and sample prompts; 4) schedule dedicated benchmark next week.
10:40 Priya: that works, thanks.
10:45 Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the docs and schedule.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "KV cache" rendered as "K-V cash" in one segment), filler words and overlaps present.
